title: What is TransactionSynchronization for callbacks (afterCommit, beforeCommit)? What is TransactionTemplate for programmatic TX?

s1_definition.profdef: `TransactionSynchronization` lets you register callbacks tied to the TX lifecycle: `beforeCommit`, `afterCommit`, `afterRollback`, `afterCompletion`. Register via `TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization(...)`. Use case: send notification ONLY after commit (alternative to `@TransactionalEventListener`). `TransactionTemplate` provides programmatic TX: `execute(status -> { ... })` — each call is an independent TX, good for batch commits and avoiding self-invocation proxy problems.
s1_definition.oneliner: `TransactionSynchronization` = lifecycle callbacks (afterCommit/afterRollback). `TransactionTemplate.execute(...)` = programmatic TX for batch commits and self-invocation-safe code.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `TransactionSynchronization` lets you register callbacks tied to the TX lifecycle: `beforeCommit`, `afterCommit`, `afterRollback`, `afterCompletion`. Register via `TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization(...)`. Use case: send notification ONLY after commit (alternative to `@TransactionalEventListener`). `TransactionTemplate` provides programmatic TX: `execute(status -> { ... })` — each call is an independent TX, good for batch commits and avoiding self-invocation proxy problems.

**One line to remember:** `TransactionSynchronization` = lifecycle callbacks (afterCommit/afterRollback). `TransactionTemplate.execute(...)` = programmatic TX for batch commits and self-invocation-safe code.

sections.s2_technical:
`TransactionSynchronization` is a callback interface you register against the active transaction via `TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization(...)`. Its methods fire at known points: `beforeCommit` just before the commit, `afterCommit` once the data is durable, `afterRollback` on failure, and `afterCompletion(status)` which runs either way and tells you whether it committed or rolled back. The typical use is sending a notification only after commit, which is the hand-rolled equivalent of `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)`. For example, inside a transfer you register a synchronization whose `afterCommit()` calls `notificationService.send(...)`.

`TransactionTemplate` is the programmatic alternative to the `@Transactional` annotation. You call `template.execute(status -> { ... })` and the template begins a transaction, runs the lambda, then commits or rolls back. Each `execute` is its own transaction, which is ideal for batch jobs that need to commit every chunk independently so a late failure does not discard earlier progress. It also sidesteps the self-invocation proxy problem, because there is no proxy involved — you control the boundary directly. A senior nuance: call `status.setRollbackOnly()` to force a rollback from inside the lambda without throwing.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India runs a nightly trade-settlement job over hundreds of thousands of trades. When it was wrapped in one big `@Transactional`, a single bad trade near the end discarded the entire night's work. Separately, the transfer path needed to notify Rajesh only after his money actually moved, but the team wanted a lightweight callback rather than a full event class.

These two needs map onto the two features. `TransactionTemplate` processes trades in chunks of 500, committing each chunk independently so earlier progress survives a later failure. `TransactionSynchronization.afterCommit()` fires the notification only once the transfer commits. The code shows both patterns on the National Bank domain with Rajesh and Priya.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Rs.50,000 transfer from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001), and a settlement batch of 1,200 trades.

**Step 1.** In the transfer, `TransferService.transfer` runs under `@Transactional`. It debits SAV2001 and credits CUR3001, then registers a `TransactionSynchronization` whose `afterCommit()` will notify Rajesh.

**Step 2.** The method returns and the transaction commits. Only now does Spring invoke the registered `afterCommit()` callback, which calls `NotificationService.send`. Rajesh is notified exactly once, after the money has moved.

**Step 3.** In the settlement batch, `SettlementBatchService` loops over 1,200 trades in chunks of 500. For each chunk it calls `txTemplate.execute(status -> { ... })`.

**Step 4.** Chunk 1 (trades 1-500) commits as its own transaction. Chunk 2 (501-1000) commits independently. If chunk 3 (1001-1200) hits a bad trade, only chunk 3 rolls back — chunks 1 and 2 remain committed, preserving progress.

**Step 5.** The job reports the total count of successfully settled trades across the committed chunks.

```
INFO  [exec-1] TransferService - debit SAV2001, credit CUR3001, synchronization registered
INFO  [exec-1] TransactionSynchronization - afterCommit → NotificationService.send to Rajesh
INFO  [scheduler-1] SettlementBatchService - chunk 1 committed (500), chunk 2 committed (500)
WARN  [scheduler-1] SettlementBatchService - chunk 3 rolled back (bad trade) — 1000 already durable
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ TransactionSynchronization (afterCommit) ═══
  TransferService.transfer() [@Transactional]
    ├─ debit SAV2001 → 950000
    ├─ credit CUR3001 → 300000
    ├─ registerSynchronization(afterCommit → notify)
    └─ COMMIT ✅
         │
         ▼
      afterCommit() → NotificationService.send(Rajesh) ✅
      (rollback? → afterCompletion(STATUS_ROLLED_BACK) → no notify)

  ═══ TransactionTemplate (per-chunk commit) ═══
  SettlementBatchService.run(1200 trades)
    ├─ chunk 1 (1..500):   txTemplate.execute → COMMIT ✅
    ├─ chunk 2 (501..1000):txTemplate.execute → COMMIT ✅
    └─ chunk 3 (1001..1200):txTemplate.execute → bad trade → ROLLBACK (only chunk 3)
         → chunks 1-2 remain durable (1000 trades settled)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
TransactionSynchronization lets me register callbacks that fire at specific points in the transaction lifecycle: beforeCommit while the transaction is still open, afterCommit once the data is durable, afterRollback on failure, and afterCompletion which runs either way and tells me the outcome. I register it with TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization. It is the hand-rolled equivalent of a TransactionalEventListener in the AFTER_COMMIT phase, and I use it to send a notification only after a transfer actually commits.

TransactionTemplate is the programmatic way to manage transactions. Instead of the Transactional annotation, I call execute with a lambda, and the template begins the transaction, runs the body, and commits or rolls back. Each execute call is its own transaction, which is exactly what I need for batch jobs. In my settlement batch, I process trades in chunks of 500 and commit each chunk independently, so a bad trade near the end only rolls back its own chunk while all earlier chunks stay committed. TransactionTemplate also avoids the self-invocation proxy problem because there is no proxy — I control the boundary directly — and I can call setRollbackOnly on the status to force a rollback from inside the lambda without throwing an exception.
